structure.overview: Mr. Isaac Smeele sought judicial review of a CRA Officer's decision denying his eligibility for the Canada Recovery Benefit (CRB) on the basis that his income did not meet the required threshold. The CRA determined that his Airbnb and car rental income was rental income, not self-employment income, rendering him ineligible. The Federal Court found no reviewable error in the Officer's decision and dismissed the application for judicial review.

sections.label: Court's Analysis of Evidence and Reasonableness

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Applicant Mr. Isaac Smeele seeks judicial review of CRA Officer's decision denying his eligibility for the Canada recovery benefit due to not meeting income threshold.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court expresses sympathy for Mr. Smeele but finds no reviewable error in the Officer's decision and dismisses the application for judicial review.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Background: CRB introduced Sept 26, 2020; Mr. Smeele applied Oct 12, 2020, received payments, then his file was selected for eligibility review in Jan 2021.

summaries.speaker: evidence
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele submitted documents showing Airbnb and car rental income in 2019, but his original 2019 tax return reported a net loss; he later applied to amend his return.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: First Reviewer denied Mr. Smeele's CRB application on Aug 5, 2021, finding he did not meet income threshold or income reduction requirement under the Act.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Second Reviewer informed Mr. Smeele in Oct 2021 that Airbnb and car rental income was rental income, not self-employment income, thus ineligible for CRB; denied application Nov 3, 2021.
idea_list: Income classified as rental, not self-employment

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele sought judicial review but discontinued it when CRA agreed to a third review to consider new information he submitted in Feb 2022, including a CRA interpretation bulletin on rental income.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele submitted affidavits describing extra services provided to Airbnb guests, arguing this made the income self-employment income, not rental income.
idea_list: Affidavits from Mr. Smeele and family

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer refused Mr. Smeele's CRB application on Mar 18, 2022, again finding income was rental income and did not meet minimum income threshold.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer found host and cleaning fees combined were below $5,000 threshold and no other income breakdown was provided; concluded Mr. Smeele did not qualify for CRB.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Attorney General requested style of cause be amended to name Attorney General as respondent; court agrees and will order amendment.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Issue is whether Officer reasonably determined Mr. Smeele was ineligible for CRB due to income threshold; standard of review is reasonableness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele bases judicial review on facts not before Officer; before CRA, issue was whether Airbnb income was self-employment or rental income; he amended 2019 return after review started.
idea_list: Original issue about Airbnb income classification

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele argued Airbnb income was self-employment based on Interpretation Bulletin IT-434RSR and provided evidence of fees and extra services; claimed Airbnb was part of professional income.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: Officer determined Airbnb income was rental income and extra services did not change that, considering the interpretation bulletin.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Before court, Mr. Smeele presented a new argument about forgetting to include a $6,000 art sale in 2019 income, supported by affidavit but no bank statement.
idea_list: New argument about art sale income

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court explains it must decide reasonableness based on information before Officer at decision time, so new arguments not before Officer are difficult to consider.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele re-argues Airbnb income as self-employment based on extra services; Officer found services insufficient to reclassify income; court finds this reasonable.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Only monetary breakdown for extra services was hosting and cleaning fees totaling less than $5,000, below the minimum income threshold.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Smeele's partner pleaded that Airbnb was more than investment, a business space for artists, but this was not supported by affidavit.
idea_list: Partner's plea about Airbnb as business

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court notes bigger business picture was not before Officer, who only had minimal evidence of extra services; Officer reasonably concluded income was rental.
idea_list: Bigger business model not before Officer

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court says if Mr. Smeele had submitted fuller business model evidence, Officer's decision might differ, but burden is on claimant and Officer not obliged to make case.
idea_list: Officer not obliged to make case

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Court dismisses judicial review application and orders no costs.
